questions.question: A student argues 'if the array is sorted, binary search works' entails 'if binary search works, the array is sorted' — swapping antecedent and consequent. Which related conditional did the student actually produce?
questions.explanation: The converse of p→q is q→p; it is not equivalent to the original, so the student's inference is invalid.

questions.question: A safety rule reasons 'if the sensor trips, the alarm sounds; therefore if the sensor does not trip, the alarm will not sound' — negating both sides without swapping. What is this transformed conditional called?
questions.explanation: The inverse of p→q is ¬p→¬q; like the converse it is not equivalent — the alarm might sound for other reasons.

questions.question: To verify 'if the checksum matches, the packet is valid', a tester instead checks 'if the packet is invalid, the checksum does not match' — negating and swapping both parts. Which equivalent form is this?
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of p→q is ¬q→¬p and is logically equivalent, so testing it verifies the original rule.

questions.question: An API accepts a request carrying a token, a signature, or both — the 'or' does not exclude the both-true case. Which connective models this?
questions.explanation: Inclusive OR (∨) is true when at least one operand is true, including when both are true.

questions.question: A latch circuit must output high when exactly one of two switches is on; when both are on the output must stay low. Which connective models 'one or the other but not both'?
questions.explanation: Exclusive OR (⊕) is true exactly when the operands differ — it excludes the both-true case.

questions.question: A proof by cases argues 'either the key is in the cache or it is not' and analyzes both branches exhaustively. Which classical law asserts p∨¬p to license the split?
questions.explanation: The law of excluded middle asserts p∨¬p is always true, legitimizing an exhaustive two-case analysis.

questions.question: Convert ¬(p→q) into conjunctive normal form — a conjunction of disjunctions of literals.
questions.explanation: ¬(p→q) ≡ ¬(¬p∨q) ≡ p∧¬q — a conjunction of two unit clauses, hence already in CNF.

questions.question: Rewrite ¬(p∨¬q) in disjunctive normal form — a disjunction of conjunctions of literals.
questions.explanation: ¬(p∨¬q) ≡ ¬p∧¬¬q ≡ ¬p∧q by De Morgan and double negation — a single conjunctive term, hence already in DNF.

questions.question: In parsing ¬(p∧q)∨r, the letters p, q, r are the leaves — variables containing no connectives. Propositional variables are also called what?
questions.explanation: Propositional variables are atomic formulas — the indivisible building blocks from which compound formulas are formed.

questions.question: To confirm p→(q→p) is a tautology without any axioms or inference rules, a student evaluates it under all four truth assignments and finds every row true. Which method is being used?
questions.explanation: A truth table enumerates all assignments; p→(q→p) comes out true in all four rows, proving it a tautology semantically.

questions.question: A SAT solver processes (p∨¬q∨r)∧(¬p∨q), treating each parenthesized disjunction as a unit that must contain a true literal. What is each such disjunction called?
questions.explanation: In CNF each disjunction of literals is a clause; satisfiability requires every clause to contain a satisfied literal.

questions.question: A fabrication plant can mass-produce only a single type of two-input gate, yet the design must still realize every Boolean function. Name one binary connective that suffices on its own.
questions.explanation: NAND alone is functionally complete: ¬p ≡ p↑p and p∧q ≡ (p↑q)↑(p↑q), so all connectives — hence all functions — are buildable. NOR works equally.

questions.question: What is the simplest equivalent form of (p∨q)∧(p∨¬q)?
questions.explanation: Distributing gives p∨(q∧¬q) = p∨False = p.

questions.question: The tautology ((p→q)∧p)→q expresses which rule of inference?
questions.explanation: From p→q and p we infer q — the schema of modus ponens.

questions.question: How many rows does the truth table of a proposition with 5 variables have?
questions.explanation: Each variable doubles the rows: 2^5 = 32.

questions.question: A SAT solver runs unit propagation on the clause set (¬p∨q), (p), (¬q∨r). Starting from the unit clause (p), what final assignment is forced?
alternatives: p, q, and r all true
questions.explanation: p=T makes (¬p∨q) unit, forcing q=T; that makes (¬q∨r) unit, forcing r=T.

questions.question: How many satisfying assignments does (p∨q)∧(¬p∨q)∧(p∨¬q)∧(¬p∨¬q) have?
questions.explanation: The four clauses rule out FF, TF, FT, and TT respectively — every assignment falsifies a clause, so the formula is unsatisfiable.

questions.question: Convert p→(q∧r) to conjunctive normal form.
questions.explanation: p→(q∧r) = ¬p∨(q∧r), which distributes to (¬p∨q)∧(¬p∨r).

questions.question: Give a satisfying assignment for the formula (p→q)→p.
questions.explanation: With p=T the outer consequent is true regardless of q; with p=F the antecedent p→q is true while p is false, making the whole formula false.

questions.question: Under the assignment p=True, q=False, r=True, evaluate ((p→q)∨(r∧¬q))↔p.
questions.explanation: p→q = T→F = F, but r∧¬q = T∧T = T, so the disjunction is T; T↔T = T.
